clue.text: A quiet river situation would be suitable

parts.note: P is piano, the musical direction for playing quietly
the Po is the great river of northern Italy
a site is a location or situation

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a peaceful riverside spot as just the right setting.
explanation.walkthrough: A, P for 'quiet', the river PO and SITE for 'situation' are laid end to end; 'would be' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something apposite is apt or well suited to the occasion, which is what suitable means.

clue.text: Like court contests featuring property

parts.note: as means like, in the sense 'such as'
a tennis match on a court is divided into sets

explanation.surface: Lawsuits in court over who owns the property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court contests' suggests lawsuits, but the court is a tennis court and the contests are SETS; 'featuring' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Assets are things of value that a person owns, their property or possessions.

clue.text: High drama of Newbolt's cricket captain's exhortation

parts.note: a play is a drama
up means high, raised

explanation.surface: A tense moment in the poem where Newbolt's cricket captain rallies his side.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Newbolt's poem Vitaï Lampada has a schoolboy captain urging his team 'Play up! play up! and play the game!'; read the wordplay as drama that is high.
explanation.definitionFit: The captain's rallying cry in the poem tells the players to try harder.

clue.text: Later step possibly taken in making gunpowder

indicators.note: possibly means this is one possible arrangement of the letters

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An instruction for a further stage in the manufacture of gunpowder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' turns LATER STEP into the answer; the definition is the ingredient 'taken in making gunpowder'.
explanation.definitionFit: Potassium nitrate is the oxidising ingredient mixed with charcoal and sulphur to make black powder.

clue.text: Hot, confused, rude passenger in the Strand, for example

indicators.note: confused means the letters of the word before it are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
rough can mean crude or rude
a fare is a paying passenger in a taxi

explanation.surface: A flustered, ill-mannered traveller on the busy London street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' rearranges only the word before it, giving THO. The Strand is a main street in central London, the classic example of a busy road.
explanation.definitionFit: A main road or busy public street through a town, like this famous London one.

clue.text: Dupe of little boys?

parts.note: Vic and Tim are short forms of boys' names (Victor, Timothy), so the phrase supplies two little boys
Vic and Tim are short forms of boys' names (Victor, Timothy), so the phrase supplies two little boys

explanation.surface: Someone asks who the children have been playing tricks on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little boys' looks like a description of children, but it supplies two pet names; 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dupe is a person who is fooled or exploited, a sufferer at the hands of others.

clue.text: Thought by many to be perfect

parts.note: an idea is a thought
L is the Roman numeral fifty, a crossword convention for 'many'

explanation.surface: Something widely believed to be flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thought by many' reads as a phrase, but it is IDEA followed by L; 'to be' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideal as an adjective describes the best imaginable, flawless or perfect.

clue.text: Victories in rising give power to Muir, in a way

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters are read from the bottom up, reversed
in tells us the pieces before it go inside the piece after it

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
HP is horsepower, a measure of power
taken as written

explanation.surface: Victories by an ascending power belong, in a sense, to a man called Muir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give power to Muir' sets the power symbol before the name; 'in a way' holds that inside the street abbreviation; 'in rising', in a down clue, turns the whole of SHPMUIRT upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Triumphs are great successes or wins, which is what victories are.

clue.text: Fool falls into French river she rubs him down

indicators.note: falls into means one piece drops inside the other

parts.note: the Meuse flows from France through Belgium and the Netherlands
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A clumsy man topples into a river in France and is towelled off by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls' and 'river' suggest a waterfall, but 'falls into' is the container signal. The definition is the whole closing phrase, describing what the woman does.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseuse is a woman who gives massages, kneading and rubbing her clients.

clue.text: Horse appears to lose its flying speed -no-one is backing

parts.note: an aircraft stalls when it loses the airspeed it needs to stay up

indicators.note: backing tells us the words just before it are read from right to left

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral I stands for one

explanation.surface: A horse seems to be losing pace and nobody is putting money on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse appears to lose its flying speed' sounds like a racing tip, but the stall is a pilot's term. 'Is backing' turns NO plus I round to give ION.
explanation.definitionFit: A stallion is an uncastrated male horse kept for breeding.

clue.text: Wilde's customary declaration

parts.note: Oscar Wilde is reported to have told a New York customs officer that he had nothing to declare except this; 'customary' plays on customs

explanation.definitionFit: The word Wilde used of himself at customs, claiming exceptional brilliance as the only thing worth declaring.

clue.text: The crew's portion is a Spanish dollar

definitions.meaning: a rowing crew is an eight, so its portion is a share of the eight
the old Spanish silver coin worth eight reals, the pirates' coin

explanation.surface: Pirates dividing their loot give each sailor an old Spanish coin.
explanation.definitionFit: The old Spanish silver coin worth eight reals; read literally, a part of a rowing team of eight.

clue.text: Quite a card, but a regular brick !

definitions.meaning: the card that beats any card of another suit in a game such as whist or bridge
an old-fashioned word for a thoroughly good and reliable fellow, also called a brick

explanation.surface: Someone describes a friend as both a real character and dependable.
explanation.definitionFit: In card games the winning suit beats all others; in old slang a dependable good sort is the same word.

clue.text: Banner found a.mile from riot

indicators.note: running riot, the letters are thrown into disorder and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A flag is discovered some distance away from the scene of a disturbance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riot' looks like a place or an event, but it signals the anagram of A MILE FROM; 'found' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriflamme was the red-gold battle standard of the early French kings, so a banner or flag.

clue.text: Transport supplied for RADA students?

parts.note: RADA is the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London; its acting students might want tutors who coach them for the stage, and the phrase also names old horse-drawn passenger vehicles

explanation.definitionFit: Horse-drawn passenger vehicles running between towns, and, read as two words, tutors training actors for theatre.

clue.text: Plant is a poisonous creeper -a German word

parts.note: the adder is Britain's venomous snake, which creeps along the ground
Wort is German for word

explanation.surface: A climbing plant turns out to be poisonous, and its name comes from German.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creeper' suggests a climbing plant, but it is the snake; the German for 'word' follows. 'Is' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Adderwort is an old name for bistort, a plant whose twisted root was thought to cure snakebite.

clue.text: Those who make fun of bargains?

definitions.meaning: people who tease or banter, who chaff others
to chaffer is to haggle or bargain, so it bargains

explanation.surface: Teasers mock other people's bargains.
explanation.definitionFit: Teasers who banter are people who chaff; as a verb the same word means haggles over a price.

clue.text: Sponsors certain draws

parts.note: sure means certain
a tie is a drawn game

explanation.surface: Backers are confident of the raffle results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draws' suggests pulling or lotteries, but here it is TIES, games that end level.
explanation.definitionFit: Sureties are guarantors who take responsibility for another's debt or conduct, like sponsors.

clue.text: August assembly in the pavilion, perhaps ?

definitions.text: August assembly in the pavilion, perhaps ?

parts.words: August assembly in the pavilion, perhaps ?
parts.note: the august assembly is Britain's upper parliamentary chamber, while the pavilion at Lord's cricket ground in London is a building belonging to Lord's

explanation.definitionFit: Britain's upper chamber of peers is an august body; the pavilion is the clubhouse building of Lord's cricket ground.

clue.text: Give one to a poor tramp?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: poor means the word is in a bad state, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A charitable suggestion to hand something to a needy vagrant.
explanation.walkthrough: I, then 'poor' rearranges TRAMP to MPART; 'to a' links.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to give or pass on, especially knowledge or a quality.

clue.text: Vocal disapproval upset stars

annotationWithheld.why: Vocal disapproval upset stars (6): BOOTES needs BOO + TES, TES coming only from 'upset' read as SET going up, so 'upset' is both reversal indicator and fodder

clue.text: Not money-making lines, apparently

parts.note: read literally, poetry given away for nothing, rather than poetry without fixed rhyme or metre

explanation.definitionFit: Poetry written without regular metre or rhyme; read as two words it seems to be poetry that earns nothing.

clue.text: Dress material is worthless -nothing in it

indicators.note: in it means the piece goes inside the word just named

parts.note: vile can mean of no value, worthless
O looks like a zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A dress fabric is dismissed as worthless with nothing to recommend it.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes inside VILE; 'is' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Voile is a thin, semi-transparent cotton or silk fabric used for dresses and curtains.

clue.text: Montague gives the city a ring

parts.note: Rome is the Eternal City, Italy's capital
the letter O is round like a ring

explanation.surface: A Montague, one of Verona's feuding families, presents a ring to the city.
explanation.walkthrough: ROME plus O; 'gives' links the definition to the wordplay. Romeo in Shakespeare is the son of the Montague household.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's young lover belongs to the Montague family of Verona, so he is a Montague.

clue.text: Picker-up of a fateful handkerchief

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Othello, Iago's wife finds Desdemona's dropped handkerchief and gives it to him, setting the tragedy going

explanation.definitionFit: Iago's wife in Othello picks up the dropped handkerchief that Iago uses to prove Desdemona false.

clue.text: "Where armies clash by night "(Arnold)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Matthew Arnold's poem Dover Beach, whose last line has armies that know nothing clashing by night; the blank before 'armies' is lost in the text

explanation.definitionFit: Arnold's line reads 'Where ... armies clash by night', the missing word meaning lacking knowledge.

clue.text: Method in Daisy's temporary madness?

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the following words, spanning the join between them

explanation.surface: There is a logic behind Daisy's brief fit of madness, echoing Hamlet's method in madness.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'Daisy's temporary'; 'madness?' completes the allusion to Polonius's line about method in madness in Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is an organised procedure or scheme, which is what a method is.

clue.text: Laws made by figures including Turkish leader

indicators.note: including means the second piece is taken inside the first

parts.note: statues are sculpted figures

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Laws drawn up by notable people, among them a Turkish ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures' suggests people or numbers, but it is STATUES; 'including' puts T, the first letter of 'Turkish', inside. 'Made by' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Statutes are written laws passed by a legislature.
